claim: βH-spectrin regulates Hippo signaling through the Jub biomechanical pathway due to its influence on cytoskeletal tension.
source: Our results establish that βH-spectrin regulates Hippo signaling through the Jub biomechanical pathway due to its influence on cytoskeletal tension.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript including Jub localization assays and genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: α-spectrin also regulates Hippo signaling through Jub.
source: While we find that α-spectrin also regulates Hippo signaling through Jub, unexpectedly, we find that βH-spectrin localizes and functions independently of α-spectrin.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing Jub recruitment and genetic epistasis experiments presented in the Results section.

claim: βH-spectrin localizes and functions independently of α-spectrin.
source: While we find that α-spectrin also regulates Hippo signaling through Jub, unexpectedly, we find that βH-spectrin localizes and functions independently of α-spectrin.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data showing distinct localization patterns and RNAi experiments showing independent localization.

claim: βH-spectrin co-localizes with myosin.
source: Instead, βH-spectrin co-localizes with and reciprocally regulates and is regulated by myosin.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing co-localization of Kst:GFP and Sqh:mCherry with a Pearson's correlation coefficient of 0.636.

claim: βH-spectrin and myosin reciprocally regulate each other.
source: Instead, βH-spectrin co-localizes with and reciprocally regulates and is regulated by myosin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that reducing βH-spectrin increases myosin levels and that altering myosin activity affects βH-spectrin localization.

claim: βH-spectrin and myosin directly compete for binding to apical F-actin in vivo.
source: In vivo and in vitro experiments support a model in which βH-spectrin and myosin directly compete for binding to apical F-actin.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo localization studies, in vitro co-sedimentation assays, and structural modeling showing overlapping binding sites.

claim: Competition between βH-spectrin and myosin can explain the influence of βH-spectrin on cytoskeletal tension and myosin accumulation.
source: This competition can explain the influence of βH-spectrin on cytoskeletal tension and myosin accumulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing reciprocal antagonism and competition for F-actin binding.

claim: The competition between βH-spectrin and myosin provides new insight into how βH-spectrin participates in ratcheting mechanisms associated with cell shape change.
source: It also provides new insight into how βH-spectrin participates in ratcheting mechanisms associated with cell shape change.
evidence: This is an inference based on the competition model and previous knowledge about ratcheting mechanisms in apical constriction.

claim: Spectrins are membrane cytoskeletal proteins generally thought to function as heterotetramers comprising two α-spectrins and two β-spectrins.
source: Spectrins are membrane cytoskeletal proteins generally thought to function as heterotetramers comprising two α-spectrins and two β-spectrins.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about spectrin structure cited in the abstract.

claim: The spectrin cytoskeleton has been described as a lattice of cross-linked, spring-like proteins that provide structural support to cells.
source: The spectrin cytoskeleton has been described as a lattice of cross-linked, spring-like proteins that provide structural support to cells (Liem, 2016; Machnicka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Spectrins were first discovered and characterized in red blood cells but are expressed in many cell types.
source: Spectrins were first discovered and characterized in red blood cells but are expressed in many cell types.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the history and distribution of spectrins.

claim: Spectrins can bind to cell membranes and F-actin, linking them together.
source: Spectrins can bind to cell membranes and F-actin, linking them together.
evidence: This is established knowledge about spectrin function.

claim: Drosophila has one α-spectrin (α-Spec) and two β-spectrins: β-spectrin (β-Spec) and β-heavy spectrin (βH-Spec, encoded by karst [kst]).
source: Drosophila has one α-spectrin (α-Spec) and two β-spectrins: β-spectrin (β-Spec) and β-heavy spectrin (βH-Spec, encoded by karst [kst]), which could potentially generate two distinct spectrin heterotetramers: (αβ)2 and (αβH)2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila spectrin composition.

claim: β-Spec and βH-Spec interact with F-actin through their N-terminal domains, which contain two actin-binding calponin-homology (CH) domains.
source: β-Spec and βH-Spec interact with F-actin through their N-terminal domains, which contain two actin-binding calponin-homology (CH) domains, connecting the spectrin cytoskeleton to the actin cytoskeleton (Liem, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: In Drosophila epithelia, β-Spec localizes to the lateral sides of cells, βH-Spec localizes to the apical sides of cells, and α-Spec localizes both laterally and apically.
source: In Drosophila epithelia, it has been reported that β-Spec localizes to the lateral sides of cells, βH-Spec localizes to the apical sides of cells, and α-Spec localizes both laterally and apically, leading to inferences that spectrin exists as lateral (αβ)2 tetramers and apical (αβH)2 tetramers (Dubreuil et al., 1997; Lee et al., 1997; Thomas et al., 1998; Zarnescu and Thomas, 1999).
evidence: This is based on previous studies cited in the text.

claim: In Drosophila ovarian follicle cells, the absence of α-Spec diminishes the recruitment of βH-Spec to the apical domain, but it does not affect the recruitment of β-Spec to the lateral domain.
source: In Drosophila ovarian follicle cells, the absence of α-Spec diminishes the recruitment of βH-Spec to the apical domain, but it does not affect the recruitment of β-Spec to the lateral domain (Lee et al., 1997).
evidence: This is evidence from a previous study cited in the text.

claim: A mutant form of α-Spec that is unable to bind β-Spec and compromised in its ability to bind βH-Spec could nonetheless rescue the lethality of an α-Spec mutant.
source: Examination in Drosophila of a mutant form of α-Spec that, based on in vitro studies, is unable to bind β-Spec and compromised in its ability to bind βH-Spec revealed that it could nonetheless rescue the lethality of an α-Spec mutant (Khanna et al., 2015).
evidence: This is evidence from a previous study cited in the text.

claim: Mammalian βV-Spec can homodimerize through its C-terminal region.
source: Experiments done with a mammalian homolog of βH-Spec, βV-Spec, showed that it can homodimerize through its C-terminal region, raising the possibility that βV-Spec might be able to cross-link F-actin by itself (Papal et al., 2013).
evidence: This is evidence from a previous study cited in the text.

claim: Spectrins regulate Hippo signaling, with effects on readouts of Hippo signaling reported in Drosophila imaginal discs and ovarian follicles, as well as in cultured mammalian cells.
source: Several studies have reported that spectrins also regulate Hippo signaling, with effects on readouts of Hippo signaling reported in Drosophila imaginal discs and ovarian follicles, as well as in cultured mammalian cells (Deng et al., 2015; Deng et al., 2020; Fletcher et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on multiple previous studies cited in the text.

claim: Hippo signaling is a signal transduction network that responds to diverse upstream inputs, including the cytoskeleton and cells' physical environment.
source: Hippo signaling is a signal transduction network that responds to diverse upstream inputs, including the cytoskeleton and cells' physical environment (Misra and Irvine, 2018; Zheng and Pan, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hippo signaling modulates cell proliferation and fate, largely through the regulation of Yap family transcriptional co-activator proteins.
source: Hippo signaling modulates cell proliferation and fate, largely through the regulation of Yap family transcriptional co-activator proteins (Yorkie, Yki, in Drosophila, YAP1 and TAZ in humans).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hippo signaling function.

claim: Yki is primarily regulated through phosphorylation by the kinase Warts (Wts), which promotes the cytoplasmic localization of Yki.
source: Yki is primarily regulated through phosphorylation by the kinase Warts (Wts), which promotes the cytoplasmic localization of Yki.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hippo signaling pathway.

claim: The Jub biomechanical pathway involves tension-dependent recruitment of an Ajuba LIM protein (Jub in Drosophila, LIMD1 in mammals) to α-catenin at adherens junctions (AJs).
source: This involves tension-dependent recruitment of an Ajuba LIM protein (Jub in Drosophila, LIMD1 in mammals) to α-catenin at adherens junctions (AJs) (Alégot et al., 2019; Ibar et al., 2018; Rauskolb et al., 2022; Rauskolb et al., 2014; Sarpal et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Jub recruits and inhibits Wts, resulting in increased Yki activity.
source: Jub then recruits and inhibits Wts, resulting in increased Yki activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Jub biomechanical pathway.

claim: Fletcher et al., 2015 suggested that the spectrin cytoskeleton influences the membrane density, and thereby the activation state, of upstream regulators of Hippo signaling.
source: Fletcher et al., 2015, focusing on βH-Spec, suggested that the spectrin cytoskeleton influences the membrane density, and thereby the activation state, of upstream regulators of Hippo signaling.
evidence: This is a claim from a previous study cited in the text.

claim: Wong et al., 2015 suggested that spectrins might influence Hippo signaling by modulating levels of F-actin.
source: Wong et al., 2015, focusing on β-Spec, suggested that spectrins might influence Hippo signaling by modulating levels of F-actin; increased levels of F-actin have been reported in other studies to be associated with increased Yki/Yap activity (Aragona et al., 2013; Fernández et al., 2011; Sansores-Garcia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a claim from a previous study cited in the text.

claim: Increased levels of F-actin have been reported to be associated with increased Yki/Yap activity.
source: Wong et al., 2015, focusing on β-Spec, suggested that spectrins might influence Hippo signaling by modulating levels of F-actin; increased levels of F-actin have been reported in other studies to be associated with increased Yki/Yap activity (Aragona et al., 2013; Fernández et al., 2011; Sansores-Garcia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Deng et al., 2015 reported that spectrins regulate levels of phosphorylated myosin light chain but surprisingly did not affect levels of myosin or recruitment of Jub.
source: Deng et al., 2015, focusing on α-Spec, reported that spectrins regulate levels of phosphorylated myosin light chain (required for myosin activation) but surprisingly did not affect levels of myosin or recruitment of Jub, leading them to infer that spectrins can act through a novel tension-dependent but Jub-independent pathway.
evidence: This is a claim from a previous study cited in the text.

claim: Deng et al., 2015 inferred that spectrins can act through a novel tension-dependent but Jub-independent pathway.
source: Deng et al., 2015, focusing on α-Spec, reported that spectrins regulate levels of phosphorylated myosin light chain (required for myosin activation) but surprisingly did not affect levels of myosin or recruitment of Jub, leading them to infer that spectrins can act through a novel tension-dependent but Jub-independent pathway.
evidence: This is an inference from a previous study cited in the text.

claim: Deng et al., 2020 reported that in the pupal eye, spectrins can act through Jub, while suggesting that the action of spectrins in the pupal eye differs from their action in the wing disc.
source: These same authors later reported that in the pupal eye, spectrins can act through Jub, while suggesting that the action of spectrins in the pupal eye differs from their action in the wing disc (Deng et al., 2015; Deng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a claim from a previous study cited in the text.

claim: Mutation or RNAi-mediated knockdown of spectrins in wing and eye imaginal discs increased myosin activity, as visualized by staining for myosin light chain phosphorylated at activation sites (pMLC).
source: Prior studies have reported that mutation or RNAi-mediated knockdown of spectrins in wing and eye imaginal discs increased myosin activity, as visualized by staining for myosin light chain phosphorylated at activation sites (pMLC) (Deng et al., 2015; Forest et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on previous studies cited in the text.

claim: It was reported that levels of GFP-tagged myosin light chain (Sqh:GFP) or F-actin were unaffected by spectrin knockdown.
source: Surprisingly, it was also reported that levels of GFP-tagged myosin light chain (encoded in Drosophila by spaghetti squash, Sqh:GFP) or F-actin were nonetheless unaffected (Deng et al., 2015), whereas changes in myosin activity generally correlate with changes in myosin accumulation (Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Noll et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a claim from a previous study cited in the text.

claim: Changes in myosin activity generally correlate with changes in myosin accumulation.
source: Surprisingly, it was also reported that levels of GFP-tagged myosin light chain (encoded in Drosophila by spaghetti squash, Sqh:GFP) or F-actin were nonetheless unaffected (Deng et al., 2015), whereas changes in myosin activity generally correlate with changes in myosin accumulation (Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Noll et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Knockdown of βH-Spec in posterior wing cells increased apical pMLC.
source: This increased apical pMLC in posterior cells, where levels of βH-Spec were reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and D), consistent with previous reports (Deng et al., 2015; Forest et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and D.

claim: Depletion of βH-Spec led to increased junctional tension as measured by recoil velocity after laser cutting.
source: A difference in junctional tension between anterior (control) cells and posterior (βH-Spec RNAi) cells in our experiments was confirmed by measuring the recoil velocity of cell junctions after laser cutting, which demonstrated an increased tension in the βH-Spec depleted sides (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Depletion of βH-Spec led to increased levels of junctional myosin.
source: We found that depletion of βH-Spec led to increased levels of junctional myosin (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Knockdown of α-Spec caused an increased accumulation of apical myosin, as well as pMLC and junctional tension, similar to the effects of βH-Spec knockdown.
source: However, we found that knockdown of α-Spec also caused an increased accumulation of apical myosin, as well as pMLC and junctional tension, similar to the effects of βH-Spec knockdown (Figure 1C, F, H, I; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The thickness of the wing disc epithelium was reduced by α-Spec knockdown, but not by βH-Spec knockdown.
source: α-Spec and βH-Spec knockdown differed though in that the thickness of the wing disc epithelium was reduced by α-Spec knockdown, but not by βH-Spec knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), indicating that even though α-Spec and βH-Spec have similar effects on junctional myosin, their roles in wing disc cells differ.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Multiple studies have consistently observed that Jub localization increases when tension at AJ is increased.
source: However, multiple studies have consistently observed that Jub localization increases when tension at AJ is increased (Forest et al., 2018; Pan et al., 2018; Rauskolb et al., 2019; Rauskolb et al., 2014; Razzell et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The increased junctional tension and myosin activity caused by βH-Spec depletion is associated with increased junctional recruitment of Jub.
source: Consistent with this, examination of Jub:GFP confirmed that the increased junctional tension and myosin activity caused by βH-Spec depletion is associated with increased junctional recruitment of Jub (Figure 2B, E and G–H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Knockdown of βH-Spec throughout the developing wing under nub-Gal4 control increases wing size.
source: Knockdown of βH-Spec throughout the developing wing under nub-Gal4 control increases wing size (wings were 116% and 119% of nub-Gal4 UAS-dcr2 control size for the two different UAS-RNAi lines used) (Figure 3A, C–D, and K; Deng et al., 2015; Fletcher et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and consistent with previous studies.

claim: Knockdown of jub leads to smaller wings.
source: Knockdown of jub leads to smaller wings (Das Thakur et al., 2010; Rauskolb et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on previous studies cited in the text.

claim: In animals with simultaneous RNAi knockdown of jub and kst, wing size is similar to that of jub RNAi wings.
source: In animals with simultaneous RNAi knockdown of jub and kst, wing size is similar to that of jub RNAi wings (Figure 3B, E–F, and K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The epistasis of jub to kst is consistent with the hypothesis that βH-Spec regulates wing size through its tension-dependent regulation of Jub.
source: The epistasis of jub to kst is consistent with the hypothesis that βH-Spec regulates wing size through its tension-dependent regulation of Jub.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic epistasis data.

claim: Simultaneous RNAi knockdown of Rho kinase (Rok) and βH-Spec reduced wing size and junctional Jub localization similar to that observed in control wing discs with Rok knockdown.
source: To further illustrate this, we reduced tension in wing discs with βH-Spec knockdown by simultaneous RNAi knockdown of Rho kinase (Rok) (Rauskolb et al., 2014; Winter et al., 2001). This reduced wing size and junctional Jub localization similar to that observed in control wing discs with Rok knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Rauskolb et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockdown of βH-Spec in posterior compartments caused a mild increase in ex-lacZ expression compared to the anterior compartment and to control posterior compartments.
source: Knockdown of βH-Spec in posterior compartments through the expression of UAS-kst RNAi under en-Gal4 control caused a mild increase in ex-lacZ expression compared to the anterior compartment and to control posterior compartments (Figure 3L and M; Fletcher et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3L and M.

claim: Knockdown of jub reduces ex-lacZ expression.
source: Knockdown of jub reduces ex-lacZ expression (Das Thakur et al., 2010; Rauskolb et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on previous studies cited in the text.

claim: Simultaneous RNAi knockdown of jub and kst reduced ex-lacZ expression, similar to that in jub RNAi cells.
source: Simultaneous RNAi knockdown of jub and kst reduced ex-lacZ expression, similar to that in jub RNAi cells (Figure 3N and O).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3N and O.

claim: The suppression of the influence of kst on Hippo signaling by jub knockdown is consistent with the inference that βH-Spec regulates Hippo signaling through the Jub biomechanical pathway.
source: The suppression of the influence of kst on Hippo signaling is again consistent with the inference that βH-Spec regulates Hippo signaling through the Jub biomechanical pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic epistasis data.

claim: When α-Spec was knocked down in posterior cells, recruitment of Jub to cell junctions was increased.
source: When α-Spec was knocked down in posterior cells by en-Gal4-driven RNAi, we observed that recruitment of Jub to cell junctions was increased (Figure 2C and F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and F–H.

claim: The increased wing size and ex-lacZ expression caused by knockdown of α-Spec were suppressed by knockdown of jub.
source: Moreover, as for βH-Spec, we found that the increased wing size and ex-lacZ expression caused by knockdown of α-Spec were suppressed by knockdown of jub (Figure 3G, H, K, P and Q).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: α-Spec regulates Hippo signaling through Jub in wing discs.
source: Thus, as for βH-Spec, and as suggested for pupal eyes (Deng et al., 2020), our observations imply that α-Spec also regulates Hippo signaling through Jub in wing discs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing Jub recruitment and genetic epistasis.

claim: βH-Spec is localized at the apicobasal level of the AJ in wing discs.
source: βH-Spec is localized, as reported previously, at the apicobasal level of the AJ in wing discs (Fletcher et al., 2015; Forest et al., 2018; Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A and C and consistent with previous studies.

claim: α-Spec is enriched in a sub-apical region just below the AJ, with slightly lower levels extending all along the lateral membrane.
source: Conversely, α-Spec is enriched in a sub-apical region just below this, with slightly lower levels extending all along the lateral membrane (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Only very low levels of α-Spec are detected in the apical plane where βH-Spec is detected, and their distributions in this plane appear to differ.
source: Only very low levels of α-Spec are detected in the apical plane where βH-Spec is detected, and their distributions in this plane appear to differ (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: β-Spec is not required for βH-Spec localization.
source: These experiments revealed, as expected, that β-Spec is not required for βH-Spec localization (Figure 5B), but it does strongly reduce α-Spec localization (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: β-Spec strongly reduces α-Spec localization.
source: These experiments revealed, as expected, that β-Spec is not required for βH-Spec localization (Figure 5B), but it does strongly reduce α-Spec localization (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: α-Spec is not required for βH-Spec localization.
source: α-Spec is not required for βH-Spec localization (Figure 5A) but its knockdown slightly reduces β-Spec localization (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: α-Spec knockdown slightly reduces β-Spec localization.
source: α-Spec is not required for βH-Spec localization (Figure 5A) but its knockdown slightly reduces β-Spec localization (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: βH-Spec depletion does not affect α-Spec localization.
source: Finally, βH-Spec depletion does not affect α-Spec localization (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: While α-Spec needs β-Spec to localize to lateral membranes, the localization of βH-Spec and α-Spec are functionally independent.
source: These observations suggest that while α-Spec needs β-Spec to localize to lateral membranes, the localization of βH-Spec and α-Spec are functionally independent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAi experiments showing independent localization.

claim: A PLA signal consistent with close association of α-Spec and β-Spec was observed in wing discs expressing GFP-tagged β-Spec.
source: A PLA signal consistent with close association of α-Spec and β-Spec was observed in wing discs expressing GFP-tagged β-Spec (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: No significant PLA signal was detected in wing discs expressing GFP-tagged βH-Spec, implying that α-Spec and βH-Spec are not closely associated in wing discs.
source: Conversely, no significant PLA signal was detected in wing discs expressing GFP-tagged βH-Spec, implying that α-Spec and βH-Spec are not closely associated in wing discs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The distinct localization and PLA results argue against the existence of (αβH)2 complexes in wing imaginal discs.
source: Together with the distinct localization of these proteins revealed by imaging, these observations argue against the existence of (αβH)2 complexes in wing imaginal discs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization and PLA data.

claim: The distribution of βH-Spec in wing disc cells appears very similar to the apical distribution of F-actin and myosin.
source: Intriguingly, the distribution of βH-Spec in wing disc cells appears very similar to the apical distribution of F-actin and myosin, and similarities between the localization of βH-Spec and myosin in Drosophila embryos have been noted previously (Krueger et al., 2020; Thomas and Kiehart, 1994).
evidence: This is based on imaging observations and previous studies.

claim: Kst:GFP and Sqh:mCherry co-localize extensively in the apical region of wing disc epithelial cells.
source: This revealed extensive co-localization between these proteins in the apical region of wing disc epithelial cells (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The Pearson's correlation coefficient score between Kst:YFP and Sqh:mCherry was 0.636.
source: Quantitation of these images yielded a Pearson's correlation coefficient score of 0.636.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the imaging data.

claim: The Pearson's correlation coefficient score between Kst:YFP and α-Spec was 0.18.
source: For comparison, the Pearson's correlation coefficient score between Kst:YFP and α-Spec (Figure 4A) was 0.18.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the imaging data.

claim: Kst:GFP and Sqh:mCherry both co-localized with F-actin, with Pearson's correlation coefficient scores of 0.641 and 0.612, respectively.
source: Both Kst:GFP and Sqh:mCherry also co-localized with F-actin, with Pearson's correlation coefficient scores of 0.641 and 0.612, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the imaging data.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Rok reduces myosin activity by reducing phosphorylation of myosin light chain.
source: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Rok reduces myosin activity by reducing phosphorylation of myosin light chain (Winter et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: In wing discs, knockdown of Rok is associated with reduced recruitment of myosin to apical junctions and reduced junctional tension.
source: In wing discs, knockdown of Rok is also associated with reduced recruitment of myosin to apical junctions and reduced junctional tension (Rauskolb et al., 2014; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), consistent with the generally positive correlation between myosin activity and co-localization with F-actin (Fernandez-Gonzalez et al., 2009; Noll et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and previous studies.

claim: Examination of βH-Spec in wing disc cells expressing Rok RNAi revealed increased levels of βH-Spec along apical junctions.
source: Conversely, examination of βH-Spec in wing disc cells expressing Rok RNAi revealed increased levels of βH-Spec along apical junctions (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Expression of constitutively activated, phosphomimetic form of myosin light chain (SqhEE) increases the recruitment of myosin to AJ and increases junctional tension.
source: This increases the recruitment of myosin to AJ and increases junctional tension (Rauskolb et al., 2014; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), but decreases the recruitment of βH-Spec to AJ, and a portion of βH-Spec instead appears in apical vesicles (Figure 6E, F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and previous studies.

claim: Expression of SqhEE decreases the recruitment of βH-Spec to AJ, and a portion of βH-Spec instead appears in apical vesicles.
source: This increases the recruitment of myosin to AJ and increases junctional tension (Rauskolb et al., 2014; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), but decreases the recruitment of βH-Spec to AJ, and a portion of βH-Spec instead appears in apical vesicles (Figure 6E, F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Myosin antagonizes localization of βH-Spec to AJ.
source: Calculation of the ratio of intensities of the anterior (control) versus posterior (experimental) compartments further confirmed our observation that myosin antagonizes localization of βH-Spec to AJ (Figure 6G–J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 6G–J.

claim: βH-Spec and myosin II localization to AJ are affected in opposite ways by changes in cytoskeletal tension.
source: Thus, βH-Spec and myosin II localization to AJ are affected in opposite ways by changes in cytoskeletal tension.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing opposite effects of tension manipulation.

claim: Overexpression of βH-Spec using a CRISPR-activator (CRISPRa) approach effectively increased expression of Kst:GFP.
source: Both imaging and western blotting of wing discs confirmed that this CRISPRa approach effectively increased expression of Kst:GFP (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Examination of myosin under βH-Spec overexpression conditions revealed a substantial reduction of myosin localization to AJs.
source: Examination of myosin under βH-Spec overexpression conditions, using Sqh:GFP, revealed a substantial reduction of myosin localization to AJs (Figure 7A, C and E–F), and a reduction in tension along cell junctions as assayed by the recoil speed after laser cutting (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: βH-Spec overexpression reduced tension along cell junctions as assayed by the recoil speed after laser cutting.
source: Examination of myosin under βH-Spec overexpression conditions, using Sqh:GFP, revealed a substantial reduction of myosin localization to AJs (Figure 7A, C and E–F), and a reduction in tension along cell junctions as assayed by the recoil speed after laser cutting (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: Apical cell areas were increased under βH-Spec overexpression conditions, consistent with a reduction of junctional tension.
source: Apical cell areas were also increased, consistent with a reduction of junctional tension (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of βH-Spec using UAS-kstEP under en-Gal4 control reduced myosin levels at AJ.
source: Overexpression of βH-Spec using UAS-kstEP under en-Gal4 control also reduced myosin levels at AJ (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), although the effect appeared weaker than that induced by the CRISPRa approach.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: βH-Spec antagonizes myosin recruitment to AJs under both increased and decreased βH-Spec expression conditions.
source: These results provide further evidence that βH-Spec antagonizes myosin recruitment to AJs and establish that this effect can be observed under both increased and decreased βH-Spec expression conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from both knockdown and overexpression experiments.

claim: βH-Spec overexpression reduced junctional recruitment of Jub.
source: Consistent with these reductions in apical myosin accumulation, βH-Spec overexpression also reduced junctional recruitment of Jub (Figure 7B, D, G, and H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) and decreased wing size (wings were 92% and 89% of nub-Gal4 UAS-dcr2 control size, for the two different overexpression constructs) (Figure 3I–K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: βH-Spec overexpression decreased wing size (wings were 92% and 89% of nub-Gal4 UAS-dcr2 control size, for the two different overexpression constructs).
source: Consistent with these reductions in apical myosin accumulation, βH-Spec overexpression also reduced junctional recruitment of Jub (Figure 7B, D, G, and H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) and decreased wing size (wings were 92% and 89% of nub-Gal4 UAS-dcr2 control size, for the two different overexpression constructs) (Figure 3I–K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I–K.

claim: βH-Spec contains two N-terminal actin-binding domains, CH1 and CH2.
source: βH-Spec contains two N-terminal actin-binding domains, CH1 and CH2 (Liem, 2016), and myosin contains an actin-binding region in its motor domain (Duan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Myosin contains an actin-binding region in its motor domain.
source: βH-Spec contains two N-terminal actin-binding domains, CH1 and CH2 (Liem, 2016), and myosin contains an actin-binding region in its motor domain (Duan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The isolated Drosophila βH-Spec actin-binding region binds F-actin weakly.
source: We found that the isolated Drosophila βH-Spec actin-binding region binds F-actin weakly (Figure 8A), in agreement with previous reports of F-actin binding by other spectrin CH1-CH2 domains (Avery et al., 2017; Duan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 8A and consistent with previous studies.

claim: Constitutively active Drosophila myosin II binding to F-actin appears stronger than βH-Spec binding.
source: Constitutively active Drosophila myosin II (subfragment-1-like protein) binding to F-actin appears stronger than βH-Spec binding, as at the same concentration a greater fraction of myosin II is bound to F-actin (Figure 8A, B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Myosin can displace the actin-binding region of βH-Spec from F-actin by ~50% at the highest myosin concentration tested.
source: We found that myosin can displace the actin-binding region of βH-Spec from F-actin by ~50% at the highest myosin concentration that we could use (Figure 8C, bottom right).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro competition assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Myosin binding to F-actin was unaffected by preincubation with βH-Spec CH domains, likely due to active myosin's higher binding affinity for F-actin.
source: Myosin binding to F-actin was unaffected by preincubation with βH-Spec CH domains (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), likely due to active myosin's higher binding affinity for F-actin.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro competition assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The binding position of the CH1 domain on F-actin sterically interferes with the formation of a strong actin-myosin interface.
source: The superimposition of both models suggests that the binding position of the CH1 domain on F-actin sterically interferes with the formation of a strong actin-myosin interface (Figure 8D'').
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 8D''.

claim: Modeling of the βH-Spec CH1-CH2 domain indicates that the CH2 domain presents additional steric hindrance for myosin binding to F-actin.
source: Modeling of the βH-Spec CH1-CH2 domain indicates that the CH2 domain presents additional steric hindrance for myosin binding to F-actin (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–B'').
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–B''.

claim: Structural modeling suggests that the binding of spectrin or myosin to individual binding sites on F-actin is mutually exclusive.
source: Thus, structural modeling suggests that the binding of spectrin or myosin to individual binding sites on F-actin is mutually exclusive, which could explain why they compete for F-actin association in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural modeling data.

claim: When βH-Spec or α-Spec levels are decreased by RNAi, levels of junctional myosin are increased.
source: In contrast to prior studies, we observed that when βH-Spec or α-Spec levels are decreased by RNAi, levels of junctional myosin are increased.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the Results section.

claim: The increase in junctional myosin levels caused by spectrin knockdown is associated with increased junctional tension and with increased recruitment of Jub to AJ.
source: This increase in junctional myosin levels is associated with increased junctional tension and with increased recruitment of Jub to AJ.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased tension and Jub recruitment.

claim: jub is genetically required for the influence of spectrin knockdown on Yki activity and wing growth.
source: Moreover, our results are further supported by the observation that jub is genetically required for the influence of spectrin knockdown on Yki activity and wing growth.
evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis experiments showing suppression of spectrin knockdown phenotypes by jub knockdown.

claim: βH-Spec and α-Spec regulate Hippo signaling in wing discs through the Jub biomechanical pathway.
source: Taken together, these observations imply that βH-Spec and α-Spec regulate Hippo signaling in wing discs through the Jub biomechanical pathway, rather than through hypothesized alternate mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing Jub recruitment and genetic epistasis.

claim: βH-Spec functions independently of α-Spec in wing imaginal discs.
source: However, our observations indicate that βH-Spec functions independently of α-Spec in wing imaginal discs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on localization and functional data.

claim: α-Spec and βH-Spec do not exhibit significant co-localization.
source: α-Spec and βH-Spec do not exhibit significant co-localization.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing distinct localization patterns.

claim: α-Spec and βH-Spec are not required for each other's localization to apical cell junctions.
source: Moreover, α-Spec and βH-Spec are not required for each other's localization to apical cell junctions.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments showing independent localization.

claim: β-Spec is required for recruitment of α-Spec to lateral membranes in wing discs.
source: This contrasts with the requirement for β-Spec for recruitment of α-Spec to lateral membranes in wing discs.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments showing that β-Spec knockdown reduces α-Spec localization.

claim: β-Spec subunits have a pleckstrin homology domain that can mediate membrane association, as well as possessing the CH domains that mediate F-actin association.
source: β-Spec subunits, but not α-Spec subunits, have a pleckstrin homology domain that can mediate membrane association, as well as possessing the CH domains that mediate F-actin association.
evidence: This is established knowledge about spectrin domain structure.

claim: β-Spec can associate with lateral membranes without α-Spec, but α-Spec does not have a way to associate with lateral membranes without β-Spec.
source: Thus β-Spec can associate with lateral membranes without α-Spec, but α-Spec does not have a way to associate with lateral membranes without β-Spec.
evidence: This is an inference based on the domain structure and localization data.

claim: An independent role for βH-Spec has been suggested in mammalian photoreceptors, where mammalian βV-Spec does not co-localize with αII-spectrin.
source: An independent role for βH-Spec has also been suggested in mammalian photoreceptors, where it was reported that that mammalian βV-Spec does not co-localize with αII-spectrin, and that βV-Spec could form homodimers, potentially allowing it to cross-link actin by itself, enabling α-Spec-independent functions (Papal et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on a previous study cited in the text.

claim: The results do not exclude the possibility that βH-Spec and α-Spec might act together in a physical complex in other tissues, or under distinct physiological conditions.
source: Nonetheless, our results do not exclude the possibility that βH-Spec and α-Spec might act together in a physical complex in other tissues, or under distinct physiological conditions.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential alternative scenarios.

claim: βH-Spec and α-Spec act independently in wing discs, implying that they influence tension at apical junctions through distinct mechanisms.
source: The conclusion that βH-Spec and α-Spec act independently in wing discs implies that they influence tension at apical junctions through distinct mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the independent localization and function data.

claim: α-Spec could influence AJ tension in wing discs through the mechanism proposed for pupal eyes, where α- and β-Spec maintain cell rigidity by linking F-actin to membranes.
source: We suggest that α-Spec could influence AJ tension in wing discs through the mechanism proposed to explain the influence of α- and β-Spec in pupal eyes (Deng et al., 2020). It was inferred that α- and β-Spec maintain cell rigidity by linking F-actin to membranes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on a previous study and the observed phenotypes.

claim: In the absence of α- or β-Spec, dissociation between F-actin and the membrane leads to an expansion of the apical regions, which increases cytoskeletal tension at AJs.
source: In the absence of α- or β-Spec, it was proposed that dissociation between F-actin and the membrane leads to an expansion of the apical regions. This expansion increases cytoskeletal tension at AJs, which bind F-actin independently of spectrins.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from a previous study.

claim: A decrease in cell height was observed in α-Spec knockdown cells in wing discs, in conjunction with increased tension at apical junctions.
source: Consistent with this suggested mechanism, we observed a decrease in cell height in α-Spec knockdown cells in wing discs, in conjunction with increased tension at apical junctions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced epithelial thickness and increased tension.

claim: The alteration in cell shape was not observed in βH-Spec knockdown cells, supporting the conclusion that βH-Spec and α-Spec act in different ways to regulate junctional tension.
source: The alteration in cell shape was not observed in βH-Spec knockdown cells, further supporting the conclusion that βH-Spec and α-Spec act in different ways to regulate junctional tension.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no change in epithelial thickness with βH-Spec knockdown.

claim: A mutual antagonism exists between βH-Spec and myosin in vivo for localization to apical F-actin.
source: We observed a mutual antagonism between βH-Spec and myosin in vivo for localization to apical F-actin: decreasing βH-Spec increases junctional myosin, while increasing βH-Spec decreases junctional myosin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from both knockdown and overexpression experiments.

claim: Increasing myosin activity decreases βH-Spec localization to apical F-actin, while decreasing myosin activity increases βH-Spec localization to apical F-actin.
source: Reciprocally, increasing myosin activity decreases βH-Spec localization to apical F-actin, while decreasing myosin activity increases βH-Spec localization to apical F-actin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using SqhEE and Rok RNAi.

claim: In vitro studies with purified protein domains revealed that myosin can compete with βH-Spec for binding to F-actin.
source: In vitro studies with purified protein domains revealed that myosin can compete with βH-Spec for binding to F-actin.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-sedimentation assay data.

claim: Computational modeling of protein structures revealed that myosin and βH-Spec would interfere with each other's binding to F-actin.
source: Finally, computational modeling of protein structures revealed that myosin and βH-Spec would interfere with each other's binding to F-actin.
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling data.

claim: βH-Spec and myosin can directly compete with each other for localization to F-actin.
source: Together, these observations indicate that βH-Spec and myosin can directly compete with each other for localization to F-actin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vivo, in vitro, and modeling data.

claim: The influence of βH-Spec on junctional tension is likely to be a direct consequence of its competition with myosin for overlapping binding sites on F-actin.
source: We suggest therefore that the influence of βH-Spec on junctional tension is likely to be a direct consequence of its competition with myosin for overlapping binding sites on F-actin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the competition data and the observed effects on tension.

claim: The CH2 domain regulates the actin binding function of the CH1 domain through steric hindrance when the two domains are associated.
source: Second, it has been suggested for β-Spec that the CH2 domain regulates the actin binding function of the CH1 domain through steric hindrance when the two domains are associated (Avery et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on a previous study cited in the text.

claim: A specific mutation in β-Spec CH2 (L253P) has been shown to lower the energetic barrier between closed and open structural states, increasing the affinity of β-Spec for F-actin around 1000-fold.
source: A specific mutation in β-Spec CH2 (L253P) has been shown to lower the energetic barrier between closed and open structural states, increasing the affinity of β-Spec for F-actin around 1000-fold (Avery et al., 2016), but it is unknown how β-Spec or βH-Spec conformational changes are normally regulated in vivo and whether both proteins share this regulatory feature.
evidence: This is based on a previous study cited in the text.

claim: Phosphorylation of myosin regulatory light chain shifts myosin from a compact, autoinhibited conformation to a filamentous, active conformation.
source: Additionally, phosphorylation of myosin regulatory light chain shifts myosin from a compact, autoinhibited conformation to a filamentous, active conformation (Kiehart and Feghali, 1986; Vasquez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The autoinhibited conformation of myosin binds F-actin very weakly (KD>100 µM) compared to the active conformation.
source: The autoinhibited conformation binds F-actin very weakly (KD>100 µM) (Heissler and Manstein, 2013; Sellers et al., 1982) compared to the active conformation, suggesting that spectrin could outcompete autoinhibited myosin more effectively than active myosin for binding to F-actin.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The competition between βH-Spec and myosin provides key insights into how βH-Spec contributes to ratcheting of apical constriction.
source: The competition between βH-Spec and myosin also provides key insights into how βH-Spec contributes to ratcheting of apical constriction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the competition model and knowledge of ratcheting mechanisms.

claim: The apical constriction of cells in the ventral furrow that initiates Drosophila mesoderm invagination occurs through fast constriction pulses interrupted by pauses during which cells must stabilize their constricted state before reinitiating constriction.
source: The apical constriction of cells in the ventral furrow that initiates Drosophila mesoderm invagination occurs through fast constriction pulses interrupted by pauses during which cells must stabilize their constricted state before reinitiating constriction (Martin et al., 2009; Xie and Martin, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ratcheting-like behavior during apical constriction is thought to be a consequence of the finite length of actin filaments.
source: This ratcheting-like behavior is thought to be a consequence of the finite length of actin filaments.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ratcheting mechanisms.

claim: Myosin contracts the cytoskeleton by driving filaments past each other, and extensive contractions require release and reassociation with new pairs of filaments.
source: Myosin contracts the cytoskeleton by driving filaments past each other, and extensive contractions require release and reassociation with new pairs of filaments.
evidence: This is established knowledge about myosin function.

claim: βH-Spec participates in ratcheting of apical constriction.
source: βH-Spec participates in ratcheting of apical constriction (Krueger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on a previous study cited in the text.

claim: When βH-Spec is knocked down, cells can undergo cycles of unratcheted apical constriction during which they alternately constrict and then expand.
source: When βH-Spec is knocked down, cells can undergo cycles of unratcheted apical constriction during which they alternately constrict and then expand.
evidence: This is based on a previous study about βH-Spec function in apical constriction.

claim: Most βH-Spec-depleted embryos fail to complete normal mesoderm invagination.
source: Consequently, most βH-Spec-depleted embryos fail to complete normal mesoderm invagination.
evidence: This is based on a previous study about βH-Spec function in mesoderm invagination.

claim: It was proposed that the actin cross-linking function of βH-Spec could hold F-actin in place for the next cycle of myosin-mediated contraction.
source: It was proposed that the actin cross-linking function of βH-Spec could hold F-actin in place for the next cycle of myosin-mediated contraction, but this raises the question of how myosin and βH-Spec association with F-actin are coordinated so that βH-Spec prevents relaxation without interfering with constriction.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from previous studies.

claim: The release of myosin from F-actin at the end of a cycle of contraction would naturally be coupled to the accessibility of F-actin for binding by βH-Spec due to their competition for the same binding site.
source: Our results suggest a simple solution: since they compete for the same binding site, the release of myosin from F-actin at the end of a cycle of contraction would naturally be coupled to the accessibility of F-actin for binding by βH-Spec.
evidence: This is an inference based on the competition model.

claim: The competition between myosin and βH-Spec for binding to F-actin enables myosin-mediated cell contraction to effectively alternate with βH-Spec-mediated stabilization.
source: Thus, the competition between myosin and βH-Spec for binding to F-actin enables myosin-mediated cell contraction to effectively alternate with βH-Spec-mediated stabilization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the competition model and knowledge of ratcheting mechanisms.
